native_result.query: Does increased time preference leads to higher BMI?
native_result.HypoA: Higher time preference associated with higher BMI for 1989 data.
native_result.WorkflowA:
1. Selected appropriate variables from the raw data
e.g.: Height: Height of respondent on 1985 instead of 1981.
      Income: Total net family income, 1989 (There are many other income variables in the raw data)
      Age:    Age of respondent at 1989 (Derived from Age at 1979).
Data Transformation:
2. Replaced -1 to -5 values (unavailable data) with NaN
3. Imputed the missing values in the AGE and INCOME variable with mean.
4. AGE_1989 had missing values, hence derived the variable as [AGE_1979 + 10]
5. Created a BMI variable using: bmi = (weight) * 0.453592 / (height) * 0.0254
6. Divided the Family income variable by 1000$ (Mentioned in the paper)
7. Created an AGE^2 variable (From the paper)
8. One-hot encoded RACE variable into BLACK and HISPANIC
9. One-hot encooded GENDER variable into MALE and FEMALE
10. Selected 'Was more money put into or taken out of R/spouse savings since last interview, 1989' as the Time Preference variable.
  DISSAVED = 1 if 'TOOK MORE MONEY OUT' else 0
  SAMESAVE = 1 if 'NO SAVINGS' or 'NO CHANGE' else 0
11. Dropped the unimportant columns for replication
12. DISSAVED and SAMESAVE as independent variables and BMI as dependent variable
13. Fit an OLS Regression Model
native_result.HypoB:
ANSWER (2-4 sentences):

In NLSY79, a respondent classified as more "patient" on the 1989 household-savings-action proxy (= saving in rather than withdrawing/holding no savings) has lower BMI in 1989 by about 0.30 kg/m² per unit shift (95% CI [-0.45,-0.14], p=1.85e-04, n=6,074, cluster-robust SE on Sample ID; standardized beta=-0.056), equivalent to ~12% lower odds of obesity (OR=0.88, 95% CI [0.82,0.94]). The same direction shows up in the forward 1992 BMI (-0.36 kg/m², p=2e-04, n=5,062), is sharper in the unmarried sub-sample where household savings is not diluted by a spouse (-0.45 kg/m², p=0.032, n=487), and survives as same-sign (smaller magnitude) in the BMI_1981 negative control (-0.20 kg/m², p=0.046). This is associational evidence on household-level savings flow, not a causal estimate of individual discount rate, because (i) no experimental time-preference item exists in the subset, (ii) the 1989 savings measure is respondent/spouse-aggregated, and (iii) three OVB sources are unresolvable from this data: no physical-activity/diet/smoking controls, no pregnancy indicator on the 1989/1992 BMI waves, and attrition that retains higher-ability respondents.

The empirical lm-coefficient ratio under "kg-pretend" vs "lb-correct" is 2.2046 — exactly the kg/lb conversion — and the only biologically plausible BMI for 14-22 y in 1981 is under the lb reading.
